evidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
evidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
evidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

evidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
evidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
evidence.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
evidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

evidence.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
evidence.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
evidence.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
evidence.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

evidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
evidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
evidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
evidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

evidence.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
evidence.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
evidence.discipline: Machine learning; Statistical learning; Data science
evidence.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
evidence.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

evidence.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
evidence.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
evidence.discipline: Machine learning; Deep learning; Data science
evidence.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
evidence.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design

evidence.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
evidence.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
evidence.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
evidence.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

evidence.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
evidence.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
evidence.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
evidence.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

evidence.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
evidence.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
evidence.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
evidence.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation

evidence.description2: Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations, including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.

Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
evidence.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
evidence.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
evidence.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

evidence.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
evidence.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
evidence.discipline: Sustainability science; Applied mathematics; Chemistry; Physics
evidence.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
evidence.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

evidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
evidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
evidence.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
evidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

evidence.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
evidence.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
evidence.topics: International state system and non-state actors; Classical and contemporary geopolitics; Realism and neorealism; Liberalism and neoliberalism; Marxism and world-systems theory; Constructivism and critical theory; Foreign-policy decision-making; War and great-power competition; Colonialism and economic relations; Climate politics; UN Security Council diplomacy
evidence.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting

evidence.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
evidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
evidence.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
evidence.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

evidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
evidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
evidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
evidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

evidence.description2: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
evidence.profile: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
evidence.topics: Modernity and Eurocentrism; Functionalism; Frankfurt School critical theory; Black feminist thought and intersectionality; Social construction of reality; Symbolic interactionism; Stigma and othering; Social space, capital and art; Coloniality and postcolonialism; Decolonial and Indigenous sociology; Gender and power
evidence.methods: Close reading of social theory; Comparative theoretical analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Visual sociological analysis; Literature-based sociological research

evidence.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
evidence.profile: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
evidence.topics: Disease frequency and risk; Incidence and prevalence; Measures of association; Epidemiological study designs; Bias, confounding and causality; Outbreak investigation; Social and environmental health determinants; Health inequalities; Health promotion; Health-needs assessment; Screening; Evidence-informed interventions and implementation
evidence.methods: Epidemiological rate and risk calculation; Descriptive and analytic epidemiology; Study-design and evidence appraisal; Population-health data interpretation; Outbreak analysis; Health-needs assessment; Stakeholder interviewing; Evidence-informed intervention development

evidence.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
evidence.profile: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Skeletal, thoracic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, reproductive and lower urinary anatomy are developed through spatial reasoning, medical images, anatomical drawing and human-specimen material. Guided practicals and dissection-room observation connect three-dimensional relationships to variation. Historical, ethical and societal questions about human remains, representation and sex accompany the anatomical study; activities are framed as academic learning rather than clinical qualification.
evidence.discipline: Human anatomy; Functional anatomy; Biomedical ethics
evidence.topics: Anatomical terminology and body planes; Medical imaging; Skeletal system and vertebral column; Thorax and pelvis; Respiratory and cardiovascular systems; Abdominal organs and vascular supply; Reproductive and lower urinary systems; Anatomical variation and intersex presentations; Human remains and dissection ethics; History and representation of the body
evidence.methods: Surface-anatomy observation; Anatomical image interpretation; Scientific anatomical drawing; Three-dimensional anatomical reasoning; Guided study of human skeletal remains and anatomical specimens; Ethical reflection on anatomical practice

evidence.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
evidence.profile: Studies how drugs act at molecular, cellular and whole-body levels and how the body handles them. Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics provide foundations for rational therapies and drug-target identification. Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.
evidence.topics: Drug discovery and targets; Drug-receptor interactions; Pharmacodynamics; Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination; Pharmacokinetics; Antimicrobial therapy; Inflammation and immunopharmacology; Autonomic regulation; Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Pharmacogenomics; Drug toxicity; Access to experimental treatments and evidence; Homeopathy
evidence.methods: Concentration-response modelling; Pharmacokinetic time-concentration and time-response analysis; Pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameter calculation; Virtual organ-bath experiments; Hypothesis and experimental-design development

evidence.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
evidence.profile: Examines host-microbe interactions and the immune mechanisms that protect against infection or cause disease. Microbiology and innate defence lead into antibodies, antigen recognition, lymphocyte development and memory, effector responses and mucosal immunity. Vaccination, allergy, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity connect mechanisms to clinical problems. Students analyze lymphocyte phenotypes using original flow-cytometry data and synthesize recent research in an extended and graphical abstract.
evidence.topics: Infectious agents and microbial virulence; Host defence and immune evasion; Immune cells, organs and cytokines; Innate immunity and complement; Antibodies and antigen recognition; MHC and lymphocyte receptors; Lymphocyte activation, development and memory; Cell- and antibody-mediated immunity; Mucosal immunity; Vaccination and viral infections; Hypersensitivity and allergy; Immunodeficiency; Autoimmune disease; Outbreak management
evidence.methods: Flow-cytometry data analysis and lymphocyte phenotyping; Clinical symptom and mechanism analysis; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Critical analysis of immunological research; Graphical synthesis of scientific findings

evidence.description2: Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.
evidence.profile: Connects normal organ function to pathophysiology across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Students integrate anatomy and physiology to explain symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnostic findings, treatment and prognosis. Published clinical cases develop differential reasoning and appraisal of diagnostic procedures. A creative assignment constructs an imaginary disease whose symptoms, mechanism and proposed treatment must form a coherent pathophysiological account.
evidence.topics: Organ-system disease mechanisms; Nutrition and digestive disease; Hematological and cardiovascular disease; Respiratory disease; Renal failure, dialysis and transplantation; Endocrine disorders; Neurological disease; Etiology and pathogenesis; Diagnosis, treatment and prognosis; Medical ethics; Rheumatic disease
evidence.methods: Clinical case analysis; Differential diagnosis reasoning; Critical appraisal of diagnostic and laboratory procedures; Integration of anatomy, physiology and clinical evidence; Mechanistic modelling of an imaginary disease; Biomedical literature comparison

evidence.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
evidence.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
evidence.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
evidence.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders

evidence.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.
evidence.profile: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
evidence.topics: Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Brain structure and hemispheric specialization; Attention and attentional blink; Memory and long-term potentiation; Emotion; Cognitive control and executive functions; Social cognition; Pain; Consciousness; Brain-behaviour relationships; Neuroscience research ethics
evidence.methods: Cognitive-neuroscience experimental design; Attentional-blink experiment; Critical analysis of scientific literature and empirical data; Research-proposal development; Scientific peer review

evidence.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
evidence.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
evidence.discipline: Cell biology; Molecular biology; Biochemistry; Biomedical science
evidence.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
evidence.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments

evidence.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
evidence.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
evidence.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
evidence.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis

evidence.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
evidence.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
evidence.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
evidence.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis

evidence.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
evidence.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
evidence.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
evidence.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision

evidence.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
evidence.profile: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
evidence.topics: Water and weak bonds; Amino acids and protein structure; Protein-biochemistry techniques; Enzyme action, kinetics, regulation and inhibition; Hemoglobin; Carbohydrates and lipids; Metabolic organization; Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; Glycogen and pentose-phosphate metabolism; Fatty-acid and lipid metabolism; Nitrogen and urea cycle; Biochemical mechanisms of disease
evidence.methods: Biochemical pathway and disease-mechanism analysis; Primary-literature review

evidence.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
evidence.profile: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
evidence.discipline: Molecular biology; Biochemistry; Microbiology; Laboratory life sciences; Bioinformatics
evidence.topics: Blood cells and proteins; Blood groups and hemograms; Aseptic culture and bacterial identification; Disinfection and sterilization; Antibiotic susceptibility; Genetically modified bacteria; GFP production and purification; DNA and plasmid analysis; PCR and restriction digestion; Protein and DNA databases; Genotype and population-genetic interpretation; Experimental reproducibility
evidence.methods: Pipetting and workflow planning; Microscopy and blood-smear examination; Blood cell counting and hemogram measurement; ELISA; Aseptic culture and purity streaking; Bacterial identification and inhibition-zone testing; Sterilization and disinfection testing; pGLO bacterial transformation; Protein extraction and chromatographic purification; SDS-PAGE; DNA and plasmid isolation; PCR; Restriction digestion and agarose-gel electrophoresis; DNA and protein database searching; Laboratory notebook and scientific-report preparation

evidence.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
evidence.profile: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
evidence.discipline: Molecular pathology; Human genetics; Molecular medicine
evidence.topics: Cell injury, adaptation and death; Acute and chronic inflammation; Regeneration, repair and fibrosis; Neoplasia; Pulmonary pathology; Leukemia and lymphoma; Genes, genomes and inheritance; Genetic variation and chromosome abnormalities; Gene regulation and epigenetics; Genotype-phenotype relationships; Genetic testing and DNA technologies; Gene-based therapies and cell manipulation; Genetics ethics, law and biosafety
evidence.methods: Biomedical literature review; Research-grant proposal design; Hypothesis formulation and experimental-control selection; Research feasibility, timeline and budget planning; Stakeholder-based ethical argument analysis

evidence.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
evidence.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
evidence.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
evidence.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study

evidence.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
evidence.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
evidence.discipline: Applied statistics; Behavioural research methods; Health research methods
evidence.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
evidence.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting

evidence.description2: The Psychopathology course offers a deep dive into the factors shaping mental health across the lifespan. Students will develop critical thinking skills, explore the bio-psycho-social approach, and gain a comprehensive understanding of mental health and its disorders. Through key concepts, research findings, and psychological assessment techniques, this course empowers individuals to promote wellness and make a meaningful impact in both personal and professional spheres.
evidence.profile: Examines mental health and psychopathology across the lifespan using a biopsychosocial perspective. Historical views, classification and assessment frame biological, psychological, cultural and social explanations of disorders and treatment. Case-based work applies diagnostic concepts to varied presentations. A structured literature-based essay investigates a focused mental-health question through explicit searching, source selection, evidence appraisal and synthesis, with optional use of PRISMA reporting tools.
evidence.topics: Mental-disorder concepts and stigma; Historical and contemporary psychopathology; Biopsychosocial causation; Clinical assessment and diagnostic classification; Stress and health; Anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders; Mood disorders; Somatic and dissociative disorders; Psychotic disorders; Eating and personality disorders; Substance-related and neurocognitive disorders; Sexuality and mental health; Childhood and adolescent disorders; Forensic psychology; Culture and emotion regulation
evidence.methods: Diagnostic case analysis; Application and critique of DSM criteria; Biopsychosocial case formulation; Structured literature searching and screening; Source-quality appraisal; Evidence synthesis; Critical evaluation of etiological and intervention models

evidence.description2: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
evidence.profile: Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.
evidence.discipline: Health psychology; Medical psychology; Clinical health psychology
evidence.topics: Biopsychosocial model; Health inequalities; Health-risk and protective behaviours; Behaviour-change models; Prevention; Stress and coping; Symptom perception; Somatic symptom disorders; Medical consultation; Shared decision-making; Doctor–patient communication; Pain; Chronic illness; Family and caregiver experiences; Quality of life; Cultural competence; Support for healthcare professionals
evidence.methods: Psychological case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of health-psychology research and interventions; Clinical-health case formulation; Interviewing-skills practice; Cultural Formulation Interview analysis

evidence.description2: Introduces key theories, methods and practices in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapy. Covers psychological assessment techniques and psychotherapeutic approaches and builds practical competencies and clinical skills.
evidence.profile: Introduces clinical psychological assessment and major psychotherapeutic approaches across the lifespan. Students study ethics, diagnostic systems, test reliability and validity, interviews, personality and cognitive assessment, then psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, systemic and integrative treatments. Training sessions develop introductory administration, scoring and interpretation skills. A psychodiagnostic case report integrates findings and treatment recommendations, while self-monitoring examines developing clinical skills.
evidence.topics: Clinical attitude and ethics; Diagnostic classification; Reliability and validity; Clinical interviews; Personality inventories and projective techniques; Cognitive and neuropsychological assessment; Behavioural and biological assessment; Psychological reporting; Psychodynamic and behavioural therapies; Cognitive therapy and CBT; Person-centered and family therapies; Integrative psychotherapy; Treatment outcomes and evidence; Child and adolescent clinical psychology
evidence.methods: Clinical interviewing practice; Introductory psychological-test administration, scoring and interpretation; Psychometric appraisal; Behavioural observation; Integration of assessment data; Psychodiagnostic report writing; Clinical case and therapy-session analysis; Reflective monitoring of clinical skills

evidence.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
evidence.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
evidence.discipline: Evidence synthesis; Meta-analysis; Applied statistics; Research methodology
evidence.topics: Systematic-review purpose and limitations; Review protocols and scope; Literature searching and inclusion criteria; Data extraction and study coding; Risk of bias; Effect-size types and transformations; Fixed- and random-effects models; Effect heterogeneity; Moderators and subgroup differences; Meta-regression; Publication bias; Research synthesis and reporting
evidence.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting

evidence.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
evidence.profile: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. Students connect theoretical perspectives to case studies, assessment and interventions at different life stages. A life-story interview with an adult over fifty applies developmental concepts through interviewing, analysis and a written report.
evidence.topics: Developmental theories; Genetics and environment; Prenatal development and birth; Infancy and attachment; Cognitive and psychomotor development; Early and middle childhood; Play and education; Adolescence and psychopathology; Emerging and early adulthood; Middle and late adulthood; Relationships and personality development; Care and developmental interventions; Death, dying, grief and bereavement
evidence.methods: Life-story interviewing; Theory-guided lifespan interview analysis; Developmental case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of developmental research and assessment reports

evidence.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
evidence.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
evidence.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
evidence.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design
